utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that the Defence wanted to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The last time when we addressed the issue of shorter working weeks, we were not aware that we received the report from the UN Detention Unit on the 19th, and that's -- that report dealt with the weight loss of General Mladic and although they retreated a bit on that issue, still, there is their recommendation to have four-day working week. So we just want to correct ourselves at that time, because at that time we were not aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And another issue, if I may. Next witness who is coming, we estimated three hours, and it might be that we will need a bit more, so we would kindly ask Your Honours to give us one extra hour, but I just spoke with Mr. McCloskey. We will finish our witnesses scheduled for this week until the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I just had on my mind to ask the parties whether they could be so efficient today that three plus one hour which makes four hours could be fit into today's schedule so if everyone would be a bit shorter, but apparently that is not -- nevertheless, I insist on the parties being as effective and as efficient as possible and then we'll see where we end, but I do understand that for the remaining of the week you will stay within the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's my understanding, and that's understanding of Mr. McCloskey as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's good to see that you agree on the matter. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. No protective measures, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the Defence and everyone in and around the courtroom. No, Mr. President, no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. Perhaps meanwhile I could use the time there. The position from the Defence in relation to the expert report of Dr. Kathryn Barr is now, if I understand well, that there is no objection to admission of the report. Is there still a wish to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I get back to Your Honours in two hours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Egbers. Before you give evidence -- you have a problem with the audio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher assist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you assist with the channel 4 follow at ... Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Egbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, I know that you are not a native English-speaking person. Nevertheless, you have chosen to testify without interpretation. If you have any difficulties, which I do not expect on the basis of your previous testimony, but please do not hesitate to address me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Ms. Hasan. Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find her to her right. Ms. Hasan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: My name is Vincent Egbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I'm a colonel of the Royal Marechausse, which is part of the Ministry of Defence of the Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall coming to this Tribunal in 2000 and testifying in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And do you recall subsequently testifying in the Popovic and Tolimir cases?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review your testimony from the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And was the evidence that you gave, your testimony, was it true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It still is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if you were asked about those same matters here today, would you provide the same information to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd offer the 92 ter statement, 65 ter 28977 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28977 receives number P1629, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I propose to leave the associated exhibits until the end, and for now if I may proceed with reading a summary of his prior evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've explained to the witness the purpose of reading it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness Vincent Egbers served in the Royal Dutch Army from 1988 to 1998. In July 1995, he held the rank of first lieutenant and severed as a platoon commander in DutchBat's Charlie Company in Potocari. His platoon was reduced from 30 to 20 men owing to VRS restrictions. The VRS restrictions on fuel, ammunition, food, and leave of personnel prevented DutchBat from carrying out its mission. From 9 July until 11 July, the witness took up a blocking position, referred to as Bravo 1, located to the west of Srebrenica town. From that position, he saw VRS tank fire on Srebrenica and on his blocking position, as well as VRS soldiers entering homes in Pusulici village. On 11 July, the witness went to the Bravo Company compound in Srebrenica where thousands of civilians had gathered. He accompanied the fleeing Muslims north to Potocari, and on their way there they were shelled to the left and right by the VRS. On 12 July, the witness escorted the first convoy of women and children and elderly men to Kladanj, though he did not know where their destination would be. En route, people in Bratunac screamed and through things at the buses. Serb soldiers were deployed along the road firing at the woods. The witness saw an anti-aircraft gun on a vehicle near Sandici, and at Nova Kasaba he saw hundreds of men gathered at the Nova Kasaba football field, kneeling with their hands behind their necks and guarded by VRS soldiers. He saw more men walking towards the football field also with their hands behind their next. On the morning of 13th July, the witness saw in Potocari men being separated from their families and taken to the white house, and women being pushed onto buses. The witness entered the white house which was guarded by VRS soldiers and was told that the these men would be taken to Kladanj. The men's belongings were in front of the house. The men looked terrified and indicated to the witness that they thought they would be killed. The witness saw a convoy of men leave escorted by peacekeepers and later learned that the peacekeepers had been prevented from continuing at Bratunac. He escorted a second convoy the following day of approximately 14 to 15 buses. En route, Bosnian Serb soldiers confiscated his helmet and vest at gunpoint. On the way back from Kladanj, Bosnian Serb soldiers at a roadblock stopped his vehicle at gunpoint and took it. He joined several other peacekeepers who had been escorting convoys in a similar way. The witness requested to speak to the commander of these soldiers to complain about what had happened, and he was taken to see Major Zoran Malinic at the school building nearby the Nova Kasaba football field. The witness prepared a written complaint and provided it to Colonel Beara, who he saw the following day. While at the school, the witness saw about 20 to 30 men, some of whom were injured, detained in a small structure nearby the school. Now, the following day he and the other DutchBat soldiers were released from the school and arrived in Potocari late on the 14th of July. That concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have any further questions, you may proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd just like to ask you about your blocking position. While you were at Bravo 1, did you come under direct attack?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. There -- there were a few T-54, -55 tanks by the Bosnian Serb Army who were entering the enclave, firing at our blocking position, so we had to -- to get rid of that position and get another position.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was anyone injured or was your equipment hit during the course of that fire?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, we had two lightly injured DutchBat soldiers, and there were some local Muslim men wounded by the same shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, the -- I'm moving on now to the VRS restrictions, and in particular the fuel restrictions. In your prior testimony, you've explained their impact on the patrols that DutchBat was engaged in. Did the fuel affect anything else, the lack of fuel?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, the fuel was in -- was necessary for generators so that we could have power, and the power could freeze our -- our food. So by the lack of diesel or fuel, we couldn't do that any more, so we couldn't drive our vehicles, and we couldn't eat the food in the freezer. So we just ate canned food.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did the lack of fuel have any impact as well in addition to food and water?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: During the fall of the enclave, we gave all the fresh water we had to the refugees who were in our compound, so the -- the fuel was controlled by the Bosnian Serb Army. They controlled how much fuel could enter the enclave, could enter UNPROFOR, and everything was -- we were very dependent on that. So the fuel -- we had -- we had some left just in case we needed to get out of the enclave. So that was in the vehicles, and that's what we used during -- during the attack on the -- on the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you have a water purification says tell me?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, we had, but only for the -- for the -- for the troops. So we could make fresh water, but we needed fuel for that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, in regards to the column that moved, the column of refugees, I'm talking about, that moved on the 11th of July from Potocari, I'm sorry from Srebrenica to Potocari, now, you mentioned that the column was shelled to the left and right of the road. Were you able to observe from the direction from where the fire came?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, it was indirect fire, so it was -- it came from the southern part of the enclave, the southern -- where the BSA, the Bosnian Serb Army was, and they were shelling by tanks or by mortars the refugees. So it came from the south. And I think it was there to keep the column moving. So it wasn't directly on the road, but it was on the left and the right side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you said to keep the column moving. Moving to where?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, all the refugees were nearby the Bravo Company, and the only way they could walk was 5.000 metres to the north to Potocari. So they had to move to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to deal with the first convoy that you escorted out of Potocari. Do you recall when you arrived at Kladanj you -- the disembarkation point was eventually in a wooded area, and you've spoken before about seeing a woman who had passed away, who was dead, there in the woods. Do you know anything about the circumstances of her death?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: The only thing I saw was that it was overcrowded, very hot, and that they were very, very feared. They didn't know what to expect, and all the buses suddenly stopped in a wood with only -- there was nothing surrounding them. So they thought that they would be killed over there, and that's the signal they made to me when they saw me walking nearby the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did the -- sorry, when you say "they," who are you referring to exactly?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: The refugees who were inside the buses, who stopped at Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And were these the women and children and elderly men?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: These were the women, children, and elderly, and it was organised by the Bosnian Serbs. So all the buses stopped over there, and three of the buses were able to move on to the disembarking point. They got out, and then those three buses, when they were empty, they had to leave, and the next three buses had to drive to this point again. So all the women and children, they didn't know what to expect, so they were terrified.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And the women and children who disembarked at this point, did they also see the dead woman, and did this have any impact on them if you observed any?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that, and they made a move with their finger from the left to the right in the neck like this. So they thought that their life would end there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many persons were on the buses in the first convoy that you escorted?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: About 60 persons for each bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, let's just stay with Potocari but move forward to the 13th of July, and I'd like you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, can I just ask a question about this dead lady. Did you observe any injuries or -- to her body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to -- okay. Let me withdraw that question. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So on the 13th of July, before you leave with convoy 4, so in the morning, can you tell us about convoy 3 which left before you did?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Convoy 3 was a convoy, a short convoy of buses with men who were gathered by the Bosnian Serbs in the white house, as I recall it. So it wasn't 14 buses. I think there were three buses of only men. They were elderly men, and I saw them stepping into the bus, and they -- they made the same signal from the left to the right on their throat, because they were sure that their lives would end, and they were offering money to me so I would have the money instead of keeping it with them, and I didn't take it, because I was sure that they would go to Kladanj as well, or they would be -- they were another -- there would be another solution for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, sir, in addition to seeing the men from the white house being taken and put on the buses, did you have an opportunity to go into the white house?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I've been into the white house at the 13th of July after I heard women screaming about the fact that their men and boys, mostly they were elder men, were taken into the white house. So I went there and my soldiers, they weren't permitted to go into the house, but because I had a rank, I just pointed at my rank as a lieutenant, and I told the Bosnian Serbs that I wanted to see what's inside the house, and there were men inside the house waiting in chambers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And would those be the men that you saw being put on the buses?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. Later on they were put into buses, and they were convoy 3 escorted by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, the last two questions are pure repetition of what we find already in the previous testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter 28978, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this sketch?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature on it, and I've made this sketch.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you've made these markings in red during the -- your testimony in the Tolimir case. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could give the witness a pointer so he could just show us a few things on this sketch.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. If you could take us through this sketch and just explain what we're looking at here and particularly the markings you've made.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Sure. This is the road from Konjevici. I'll just surround this here. And the roadblock was here. So we came from this direction and were stopped by the Bosnian Serb Army at the roadblock, and that's where they took the vehicles, and the vehicles were put here on a square nearby the school. And we were waiting here nearby the road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another colour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that would have been perhaps preferable, because we're now marking an already-marked sketch with the same colour, so it's unclear now. Let me just try to summarise. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we better erase the new markings and keep the old ones. The old ones are in the relevant 65 ter number, and restart and give the witness a different colour. Now, usually different colours are used for Prosecution and Defence, but I don't know how many colours we have, as a matter of fact. Perhaps we could not use the blue and the red but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The green.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The green, for example. Yes. Could -- could we first get back to the original one and not store the new markings. So we're now back at the original one, and whenever you add something, you'll take care that it's clear on the record. Perhaps you restart. I think you said the road to the right was to Konjevic. You marked that. Could you do that again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. This is the road going to Konjevic, and we came from Kladanj, from this side, and we were stopped here at the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The roadblock is in the middle between the two green circles --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- within the red circle --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with a green marking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And when I was stopped there, my colleagues were here waiting for what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness marked four crosses where his colleagues were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I had to step out of the car, and I took the car to the square as I already mentioned, and I'll underline the word "Square," and that's where the vehicles were parked, and I asked to get in touch with this -- the commander of -- of the troops who stopped me, and the commander used a school as his headquarters. Here's the school, and this is the stairs towards the school. And that's where I met this major. And only the way between the road and the school there was a house where they had men and boys captured. And here in the gym, beneath the gym there were dogs, Bosnian Serb army dogs. And in your sketch, it's Nova Kasaba but there -- the football field I'm referring to is on the side there. Not on scale, of course, but there is the football field where I saw all the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness marks a kind of a small football pitch --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the upper right hand to indicate the direction where the football pitch was found.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So that we don't lose these markings, I'd offer this marked version into evidence, 65 ter 28978.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the sketch which was marked already in red in the Tolimir case with now further markings in green would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P1630, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1630 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, you've marked the road at the top of this sketch Simici-Konjevici and you've previously described in your prior testimony the route that you took to Kladanj and back, describing it as a route from Konjevic Polje to Milici onwards. Are you -- is it the same road you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It's the same road.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: How far do you recall the -- the Nova Kasaba football field being from the roadblock that you've -- you were stopped at?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: A few hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we now see 65 ter 4950, please. May I ask that we just have that rotated 90 degrees to the right, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, you probably recognise this aerial image as it was shown to you in the Krstic case. I'd just like you to take the pointer again and -- and tell us if you can identify any buildings on this, on this aerial image.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is the road that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be better to avert confusion also to take green for marking for this one, otherwise --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we'll never know what was marked when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we get back to the original one without a new red marking. Could you please mark in green again where you say the road was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we were stopped here, the roadblock. And this is the school. And this is the way from the roadblock towards the school. This is the square. And -- and the men and boys were in one of those buildings. I don't -- I don't really -- I can't see which building it is, but in one of those buildings on this side of the road. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness marks with some dots --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to the left of the road between the roadblock and the school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I can't recall which house it was where the boys and men were captured. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm just going to show you another image, but if we could just --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If I could just offer this marked aerial image into evidence, 65 ter 4950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 69 -- document as marked by the witness receives number P1631, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1631 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could briefly look at Exhibit P01132, e-court page 40.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, I don't know if this helps you better identify where the small building or structure was that the men were kept in. If it doesn't, then it's just a better quality image. If it doesn't, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't recall which building it exactly was. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. I'd like to ask you whether you made any observations about the communication lines that were available to the school that you were taken to, the temporary barracks there.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, the Bosnian Serb soldiers who were there didn't want us to use our communications in the vehicles because they were sure that that wasn't safe. We did, but we didn't openly use them. And they were using wires to communicate, so I saw a lot of wires where telephones could be attached on. So it was possible for them to speak with others so there can't be anyone else listening with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And where were these wires running from? Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I saw them in the nearance [phoen] of Nova Kasaba at -- at various spots, and also here at the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you talk about nearance, I saw in the previous transcript that you are referring to it being near to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Being near to, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. May we have 65 ter 25663A displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Witness, I'll just ask you, this is -- we can have the English and the B/C/S, but I'll ask you if you'd like a Dutch copy. This is your 15th July report.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. We see here at the very top that this document is dated the 15th of July, and it provides that it's from 1st Lieutenant Egbers and to head of S2/34. Now, before we go into any of the detail of the document itself, can you tell us what it is, whether you prepared this document, and a little bit about when and where you did this?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I've made a report to the S2, that is the head of the section 2 who was in charge of intelligence, and head of section 3 is operations, and 4 is logistics. So it's just a report for my DutchBat colleagues which I wrote on July 15, 1995. After being at Nova Kasaba for a night, and I wanted to report what this Major Malinic told me. So that -- that's the report. Immediately after I came back at -- at the compound, I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you said the document was numbered S2-34. Now, it's numbered that way both in the English version and in the B/C/S version, but I do not know why that's different from the original version which says S2-3, without a 4. Apparently there is some transcription error.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And since you specifically referred to the number. Otherwise, I might not have noted it, but it's not vital --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as long as the content which seems to be the same so therefore please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. So let's look at what you reported, specifically item 2. It reads a number of incidents occurred between Potocari and Nova Kasaba. Vehicles, helmets, and flak jackets were taken. We can just stop there. Can you elaborate and explain where these vehicles, helmets, and flak jackets were taken as you report here?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, along the road there were Bosnian Serb troops facing the enclave on the road, and when they saw our vehicle approach, they would point their AK-47 at us, so we had to stop, and they took what they could get. So our helmets, our bullet-proof vests. That's what they wanted, and they just put their gun on our heads and we have to give it to them. That's the reason why we didn't take any weapons the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And when you refer to this taking place along the road, what road are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It's the road from Potocari to Bratunac, from Bratunac all the way to Kladanj near Nova Kasaba, there were the troops, but most of these incidents were in the first stage of the -- of the travel between Bratunac and the first big crossings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, this is also repetitious to the statement. The witness in his previous testimony said that he was stopped several times and only at one of the later stops that they were -- the flak jackets were taken, the helmets were taken. It's all in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just trying to link what's in this report with what in fact he's testified to before. He's never testified in Krstic about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But I'll move along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may be true, but it's of course pretty obvious that it's about the same. If that's your purpose, then you could have asked whether this reflects what we found already in his testimony about it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, based on your experience, your own experience and what was reported to you, did this conduct appear to you to be a random occurrence or was it a pattern of stripping and stopping and disabling of the UNPROFOR peacekeepers?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, this was a pattern. We -- all our vehicles were stopped, and they -- this wasn't just an incident. There were a lot of incidents together.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, in this same item in brackets it says "see statement in Serbo-Croat." Now, you do in your prior testimony discuss a complaint letter that you wrote up at the barracks or the school where you met Major Zoran Malinic. Is that the same statement that you're referring to here?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, in item 5 we go down, there you report on what you've also testified about in relation to your contact with the local commander, and you specifically reference him here, Major Zoran Malinic, born 1961. How, first of all, did you know he was a major as you recorded here?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That is what he told me, and I saw it on -- on his own door of his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what about his date of birth?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That was in the original Serbo-Croatian statement that we wrote in English. I don't know whether it's correct, but that's what they told me then.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, who told you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I was there with an interpreter who could speak English, write English, but also speak Serbo-Croatian, and he finished the report together with me so I could give that to Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So then the information contained for example in this item was information you learned at the time when you were drafting your complaint letter with the Serbo-Croat interpreter?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you know Major Zoran Malinic before you met him on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I've never seen him before. I haven't seen him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's move to item 8. Now I'm particularly interested in the last line there. You're -- you're referring to again Zoran. I take it that's Major Zoran Malinic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And it says here his superior commander Colonel Beara was going to get involved in the matter. Who provided that information to you first that -- that Colonel Beara was Major Zoran Malinic's superior commander?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't know whether that he was his direct commander, but he told me that Colonel Beara was the colonel in charge of the surroundings in Nova Kasaba, not on the school. So -- and of course he was as a major had to rely on this colonel, but I don't know whether there was a direct link between them, whether he was a member his force. I don't know that, but there was -- there was a relationship between them, because he was there at Nova Kasaba in the school and this Colonel Beara was responsible for the surroundings including the school. So I don't know whether this colonel was the military commander of Major Zoran Malinic. I don't know that, but that's what he told me, that he wasn't able to guarantee our safety outside his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And so are you drawing a distinction between formal chain of command versus what you had understood from what you were being told?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know whether Colonel Beara was the commander of this major, but he -- he had influence in the territory that we were moving back to the -- to the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did Major Zoran Malinic refer to Colonel Beara as his superior?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: He told me that he couldn't guarantee our safety, but this Colonel Beara could, and he was trying to get in touch with him, and he wanted to give our complaints to this Colonel Beara because this Colonel Beara was in charge of Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the second day you were at the school, the 14th of July. You encounter Colonel Beara. He arrives at the school. Now, in item 9 is -- is that what you're referring to there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I've met him, but very shortly, and he -- he went to Major Malinic immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And just to clarify, when you have here recorded Colonel Beara, how did you -- how did you know, for example, how to spell his name?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Because it was all spelled in the form that we -- the complaint in Serbo-Croatian that we made.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you communicated with Colonel Beara that day. How were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Through the interpreter. He was with me. He spoke English. I saluted him. I handed over the complaint. He tried to get us as fast as he could towards Colonel Malinic, and later on he left.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, you say he tried to get as fast as he could to Colonel Malinic, meaning he tried to see Major Malinic, he was in a hurry to see him?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, he didn't have the time to speak with me about the complaints I had. He didn't -- he didn't take the time. He had the time, but he wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall how long your conversation -- how long Colonel Beara remained at the school there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I recall that it's longer than half an hour, but I don't exactly know how long, but not -- not just going in and out, but he was there for a chat. He was there to -- to get in contact with Major Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you know when Colonel Beara left what direction he left in?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him leaving in the direction of the Nova Kasaba football field, towards Potocari, Srebrenica, that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, in item 10 in this document, you provide: "I wrote him what had happened to us which was written down. Colonel Beara has the original. A copy is held by section 2-3." Again, is that the same Serbo-Croat statement that you put together with the Serb interpreter who were present there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you keep a copy of that yourself, the complaint letter?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No. I gave the complaint letter to my superiors in the enclave, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. If we now skip to item 11. Here you -- it appears you're relating an incident that occurred where you encountered a vehicle of the International Red Cross, and you have testified about this before. Now, I'd like to ask you about some digits there on the second line in the English?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And it says "Stopped," and then it has those digits. Could you explain those digits to us, please.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Sure, that's the exact date and the exact time. So 95 refers to the year, 07 to the month, and 13 to the date. And it was at 1600 hours. So at 1600 hours on the 13th of July, 1995, two men and two women in a car stopped. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, if we continue, it says when it became -- the last sentence, "When it became clear that it was not safe they turned around and," if we can turn to the next payment, please, "and headed for Pale. I pointed out the hundreds of POWs on the football field in the area of JNA," and you have some digits there "but that did not help." What is the JNA number?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, that's a coordinate on the map, so when you have a map you can -- you can see exactly what -- what I mean. It's how military officers communicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So you're reporting to these persons about the prisoners you had seen at the football field, and this is taking place on the 13th of July at approximately 4.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall around when you would have seen the men at the football field?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, I saw them that morning when I drove with my vehicle towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you informed or did you learn that General Mladic was at the Nova Kasaba football field on the afternoon of the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I haven't seen him, and I wasn't informed that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we can now look at item 12. If we can turn the page in the B/C/S version, please. Okay. Here you talk about a house 75 metres from the school building. Prisoners of war were being held. Are those the prisoners we briefly discussed?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. They were inside the house near the school at Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, does anything in this paragraph assist you in determining when you saw these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I have the same numbers. As you can see, it was 95. It was 14 July 1995, at 1500 hours that we visited them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether those prisoners were there on the 13th of July when you were present at the school premises?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I saw them, but there were also men, Muslim men, walking in the nearance with hands on their heads guided towards several places, and I don't know whether these men came on the 14th of July, but they were there on the 13th of July, people inside the house as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, when you were given permission to go inside this small building, were you alone?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No. I was there with two other DutchBat soldiers, and there were Bosnian Serb soldiers as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could skip now to item 14 on the following page. In item 14 here, the last sentence you talk about two young POWs were taken in the direction of the escape route of the BiH fighter. Now, you have testified about two young boys who were taken from a building and used as shields. Are these the same young POWs that you have reported about here?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And approximately how old would you say these two boys were?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Fifteen, sixteen years.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: When you were ultimately taken back to Potocari, do you recall whether it was still light or dark outside when you left the school compound?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It was almost talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Does any information in this report assist us in determining when you would have arrived in Potocari on the -- when you were given permission to ultimately go back there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, I wrote down that we reached the compound at 2115, as you can see on the last numbers. So it was 14 July, 1995, 2115 that we were there, and I said in the sentence before that unfortunately, we had to leave behind two Mercedes vehicles with two numbers, so the S-10 is a vehicle and S-52 is not a vehicle, and we couldn't take them with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I think you testified about that. And this is all in item 15 on this document. Now, Witness, when you arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a short correction for the transcript. You said S-10 was a vehicle and S-52 was not a vehicle, but I don't see an S-52. I only see C-52.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're correct, but it's -- it's another vehicle. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Potocari at 9.15 on the 14th of July, were there any refugees left to escort?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Only the sick and wounded who were in the hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: There were no other refugees left?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No refugees inside the compound, nor outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. It's time for the break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I haven't yet tendered the associated exhibits. Would you like me to do that now or wait until after the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether there will be any debate about it or whether it's -- perhaps we take the next two minutes to -- if you just mention them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So the first one would be 65 ter 4951.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Photograph of a school. No objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P1632, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1632 is admitted. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will go back to 65 ter 4950 and offer that in even though we've used the same exhibit here today and the witness has marked it, but for the purpose of understanding the Krstic testimony it might be helpful to have that as well. So that's 65 ter 4950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the photograph with -- without markings, I think. Is that -- let me see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 04950.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04950 receives number P1633, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is the unmarked version of what has been admitted as 1631. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The next one would be 65 ter 5144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 5144 receives number P1634, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1634 is admitted absent any objections. Madam Registrar -- Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Finally, 65 ter 5145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Map of Srebrenica. I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 5145 receives number P1635, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1635 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, what about the document, the report written by the witness, 65 ter 25663A.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. I've omitted that one and I'd offer it into evidence, 65 ter 25663A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25663A receives number P1636, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1636 is admitted into evidence. We take a break, and we resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Ms. Hasan, Madam Registrar draws my attention to the fact that 04951, photograph of the school at Nova Kasaba with a car on the road, was already admitted as P1572. Would you please verify that. That is an associated exhibit not marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. That appears to be the same photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then P1632 is vacated. Apologies, Mr. Egbers, for dealing with other matters when you entered the courtroom. Mr. Egbers, you'll now be cross examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me begin with the kind of weaponry that was in the possession of Muslims in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have the English transcript. I can only read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can only read it. You should be at channel 4, but the usher will assist you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let us begin with whether Muslims in Srebrenica were armed, and if so, what kind of weaponry they had. In your opinion, were Muslims in the Srebrenica enclave armed?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. When we entered the enclave, all the weapons were at the weapon collection point in Srebrenica, but after Observation Post Echo fell, I saw Muslims wearing weapons inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, these weapons that you later saw in the hands of Muslims, were they previously owned by the Muslims and did they fail to hand them in, or did they import them after you entered the enclave? Did you make any conclusions about that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I can't tell you whether the weapons were there or were imported during my stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information on the number of Muslim fighting men in the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No. I saw not more than 10 or 20 armed men together at a few times, so I can't tell you whether there were more or less than 100 people carrying guns in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I should like to show you now a document marked here as D18. As you see, this is a document from the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is addressed by the commander of the General Staff, and it's dated 30th of July, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 4 of this document in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an overview, a summary, from which we can see that, for instance, 374.982 rounds were sent into Srebrenica, calibre 7.62- and 7.9-millimetres; 436 grenades; 131 rifle grenades; 292 RPG-7s, also 59 projectiles; 1 rocket launcher 107-millimetres, and 28 rockets for it; and so on and so forth. We see how many automatic rifles were sent into Srebrenica, 150. Six mortars. Were these weapons stored in the DutchBat depot at the time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I can't recall that. I haven't been inside the weapon collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Muslim forces in the Srebrenica enclave handed in to DutchBat only handmade weapons and weapons that did not work any more?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I didn't know that, but I don't know whether it's true, because I wasn't in the weapon collection point. I haven't been there, so I can't tell you whether this is true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw artillery weapons with your own eyes towards the end of your stay in the enclave; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: At Bravo 1, I saw a small piece of artillery. I don't know whether you mean this piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean. Was that piece of weaponry there from before, or did it get into the enclave towards the end of your tenure?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I've only seen it when I was in the blocking position Bravo 1, and they told me that it was there for a longer time, but we never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the weapons in the possession of the Muslim forces in Srebrenica were hidden from you, from members of the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: During the first -- the first month that we were in the enclave, we saw a few Muslim fighters wearing weapons and we tried to confiscated them. So that's what we saw. And I saw only this piece of M-48 at the blocking position number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, one of the inherent problems of hiding something is that you don't see it. So to ask whether something is hidden, unless you are seeking specific information about knowledge of the witness later that something was hidden from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We want to establish whether members of the DutchBat turned a blind eye or they didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then why not ask whether they turned a blind eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's my next question, but the gentleman said that he didn't know, so that's then he didn't know, they didn't turn a blind eye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now better understand what you wanted to ask from the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A more direct approach would have given a quicker answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see a tank in the possession of Muslim forces in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not have the right to search houses either in Srebrenica or the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. That was a discussion, whether we could follow an armed man inside a house. It wasn't -- we were not able to -- to go into the house without the police force, but I didn't -- I never went in that situation, but DutchBat troops talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether any members of the DutchBat entered into a Muslim house together with the police to search it?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I'm sure -- I'm sure other units did so, but I didn't, and my unit didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us which unit it was that entered and searched Muslim houses in Srebrenica escorted by the police?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I know that that discussion was with our special forces, and we had two members of the British SAS serving in the enclave who also participated in these actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's begin with these members of the SAS. Concerning this artillery weapon we mentioned, members of the Muslim armed forces told you that they had only a few shells; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That is correct. I saw only a few shells, because I was next to the piece of M-48 at Bravo 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't check whether they had ammunition for that artillery weapon in some other place, did you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No, we did not, but I can only tell you that it didn't fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that at any rate, it was your obligation to put that weapon in the weapon collection point overseen by the DutchBat, or you don't agree?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I was told by the Dutch Battalion commander that he opened the weapon collection point when the Bosnian Serb Army attacked the enclave, and all the weapons were inside this weapon collection point. So I had no need to confiscate a piece of artillery and bring it to a weapon collection point because the doors were open and everybody could take the weapons if they wanted to, but the Muslim fighters had no interest in using these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After you left was this weapon collection point vacated or were there weapons remaining inside?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I left the town of Srebrenica when I ordered all my soldiers to go out of the ACP, and I had a lot of injured people from the hospital inside my ACP -- I'm sorry, armed personnel carrier, and I left for Potocari never to go back to Srebrenica again. So I don't know whether there were weapons inside this weapon collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just clarify when the weapon collection point was opened? Around what date did it become possible for people to come in and take weapons out?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I only got the information that that was the meaning of the commander of DutchBat, that he would open it. I don't know whether he actually opened the weapon collection point, that was the information given to me at the time. So I don't know, and it should be in other files, think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Members of the DutchBat carried out the orders of their commander. Of course, if he issued an order, then they must have carried it out, namely opening the weapon collection point. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No. He offered the Muslim fighters to open the weapon collection point if they wanted that and needed the arms inside the weapon collection point, and they didn't need those weapons. They didn't. They had the opportunity, but they -- that's my information. They didn't want us to open the weapon collection point for their own reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you know the 28th Division of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was inside Srebrenica? It was based there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I haven't seen any division or division commander. I only saw Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you that members of this division, Muslim fighting men, were launching offensive operations against Serbian villages around Srebrenica and against Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't know whether -- there were a few men, two of them, who told me that they went outside the enclave at night and tried to -- to come back with weapons, but I don't know whether these men were a member of this division that you refer to in your -- in your question. So I spoke to people, and I asked them, "How do you -- how do you become the owner of this rifle?" And then he said it once belonged to a Serb. Did I answer your question enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at the document before us, and we will see some more, would you agree in light of this document that Muslim fighters received weapons from their command?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I think this is an excellent question for -- for -- for the Muslims, Muslim fighters or the -- the people who reported this, but I can't give you any more information, because I've seen -- I've never seen this document before. And you asked me if I can clarify this or -- because I haven't seen it, and I haven't seen all those things inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any complaints from the Serbian side that Muslim fighters were launching offensive actions against Serbian positions and Serbian settlements?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I've talked about this with Major Zoran Malinic after he met me in the school at Nova Kasaba, after the enclave fell. During my stay from January until June in the enclave, I never had contact with the Bosnian Serb Army. So when there were any complaints, they were directly to the commander of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you did not know either the structure or the strength of the Muslim armed forces inside the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I saw, and I saw a few fighters wearing uniforms. They were carrying weapons, RPGs, as I've mentioned, and AK-47s. They communicate by writing each other notes. So I have seen some of the people who tried to defend the enclave, but I haven't seen any division inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we now call up in e-court 65 ter 17856, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just for my understanding of the document which we've seen before about the supplies, do we have a time-frame for it? It's clear that it ends in -- at the moment of an accident in May. Do we know where it starts? Is it about three months? Is it about two months? Is it -- do we have any position on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that there is explanation like that in this document, so I cannot give you a time-frame for which this document is meant to describe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which of course interpreting that's apparently what you're aiming at to establish how many weapons there were. If this would have been 20 years, some of them might have been used already. Now, I take it it's not 20 years, but at least for my understanding and for the evaluation of the evidence, it would certainly assist if I would know what -- what time period this activity covers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I tried to clarify with the witness whether this armament entered during his stay or before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He doesn't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- then he could -- I didn't know that he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if someone says I saw a few soldiers walking around with a few rifles and I saw one piece of artillery, then to expect that he was fully aware of -- of this stuff being imported at that time, is, of course, a, well, a very optimistic view of what a witness could know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see before you a part of the document reflecting Dutch debriefing on Srebrenica. On page 1, paragraph 4, we see a part of your testimony. You say: [In English] "The UN patrols were regularly fired at here by persons unknown. The witness thought it likely the Muslims were responsible in an attempt to provoke the UN patrols to take action against the Bosnian Serb Army. He thought it unlikely that it was the Bosnian Serb Army firing at them, as they were not -- as they were too far away." [Interpretation] If you were asked the same thing today, would you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: And what is the question that you have for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at that time Muslim forces, according to you, opened fire at DutchBat patrols in order to provoke members of the DutchBat to open fire against Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, but what we thought happened as well was that -- that there was fire from inside the enclave towards the BSA posts so that the BSA could react on us as well. So we were provoked. And I think it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what you read to the witness is what he thought to be likely. You put it to him as if he would -- that would be correct. Do you mean that it's correct that he thought it to be likely or that he has any knowledge which would be one step further than what we find in the document? Is this an assessment, Witness, of likelihood, or is it -- do you have facts to your knowledge which could support your idea that this was the likely event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We don't have the facts. We only have the feeling that this could happen, that Bosnian Muslims were provoking the BSA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you considered that even to be likely that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just got help from my colleague Ivetic regarding the 18, the document we had previously on our screens when you inquired about that period of time which that document addressed, and my colleague did a more thorough investigation of the document than I did, and it says that this quantity of ammunition was imported into the enclave from the autumn 1994 until May 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That certainly helps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time you said Serb tanks opened fire. Is it correct that you were not sure whether they were opening fire at you or at the Muslim artillery weapons positioned in the immediate vicinity of your APC, which was placed where it was placed in order to block Serb forces from advancing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So sorry, Mr. Lukic. When you say "at that time," can you give us what time you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When they took blocking position against Serbian forces that were entering the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know where you're referring at, and when my commander asked me, "Are you absolutely sure that they are hitting UN vehicles and UN personnel?" I couldn't say yes because there was this piece of artillery nearby. So that's why my commander gave me the direct instruction to go back again. And when we were back at the hill with our white vehicles wearing blue helmets and the tank shot again, then I was sure that they shot us. But not at the first time, because the piece of artillery was in our nearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that your APCs was not directly hit, neither the first nor the second time?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It's true that there was no direct hit, but there were pieces of artillery inside the vehicle. So there was no direct hit, but it was in the nearance of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Muslim fighters tell you on that occasion that they had succeeded in destroying the Serbian tank?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I met some Muslim fighters who went to the south from blocking position 1 in order to -- to destroy a tank, but I don't know whether they succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you that they succeeded in doing so?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I can't recall that sharp. Perhaps you have it in one of my testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. I will try to refresh your recollection, and I would like to see 1D1041.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we looked at the document earlier, the debriefing document. Let me see. That is -- could you repeat the number? Is that admitted, or I may have missed it. Do you tender that, or did you just read to it? The reason why I'm asking is the following: That debriefing document most likely originally is in Dutch. Even a portion which is attached, the last two pages, is the same document as we looked at earlier, the two pages about the S2-3 or 3-4 number. I don't recollect immediately now the number, but there we had a Dutch original and the English translation and the B/C/S translation. As for this one, we do not have the Dutch original, we only have an English translation and a B/C/S translation, but to some extent at least part of it is the same document as was used by the Prosecution before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer standing here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no, but I just draw your attention to the fact that you are using documents that some of them are in evidence which are attached to other ones with or without translations, and to the extent you want to use it, I would appreciate if we have all the versions available.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will. I think that for some others in my questions, I do have all three versions, but for this one I have only two versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you don't tender it. You just read it to the witness and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and we'll leave it to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need 1D1041, which is your testimony of 20 October 2006, in the Popovic case. We need page 29 in e-court. You're talking about this very incident on the previous page. In line 7, this is your answer, and I'll read it out in English: [In English] "A. Well, I can't be sure that they really succeeded. They told me that they did. That's what they told me, but I had no vision of it, so you'd better ask the BSA whether it's true or not." [Interpretation] My question was if you remembered them telling you that they had succeeded in destroying the tank.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I can only quote what you have just read to us and that's it. I can't -- I can't say anything more than this. But I think you asked me this question, so you can have this in the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I do, but we have to have it in our trial as well. Thank you. [Interpretation] We'll move on to a different topic now. Upon your arrival in the enclave, you were taken prisoner by the Muslim forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I had no -- I could not move the way I wanted, so I was in my vehicle for some time, but being a prisoner of the Muslims, I've -- I've told you in the Krstic case about the Bandera Triangle. I think that you're referring to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I had a role in -- I then had a role in entering the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct that they kept you prisoner for two days in this manner?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: We entered the Bandera Triangle, and we were forced to stop. There were no guns openly pointed at us, but they told us to stop and to negotiate with the Dutch Battalion commander, whether to go inside this Bandera Triangle. So I was there inside the Bandera Triangle and I couldn't move, but you're calling me a prisoner. And only -- the thing I can say is that we were armed. We had our arms, and we couldn't move the way we wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that following this incident members of the DutchBat were no longer able to gain access to the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: As I can remember, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to call up in e-court P1421. It's an order by Major Franken, issued to Captain Groenewegen on 9 July 1995. In paragraph 1, the content of the order is given. Were you able to read the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: You only need me to read the assignment or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were able to hear during the testimony of your other colleagues what a "green" task or a "green" assignment meant. Is it correct that at the time, the 9 July 1995, members of the DutchBat openly clashed with the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: You refer to July 9th?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: And could you help me what happened that day? Was there an observation post taken ever by the BSA or? Because I wasn't there and you asked me whether I know this order. I think -- is it dated 9th of July as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: So I haven't been in a fight with the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you have any knowledge about your commander having called upon NATO to bomb the Serb positions around the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. That was told by my commander that there should be a gunship coming from NATO. So that's why we had to be so visible with our white vehicles. But it never came.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will take this in chronological order, and I will start from the 8th of July, 1995. Is it correct that the Muslims fell bombs that landed between the vehicles which you were moving along in? And I mean on the 8th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I can recall that I was joining the battalion reserve for APCs, and we were going south, and there were hand grenades thrown at our positions. At that time, I -- it could be the 8th of July. I'm not sure about that, but I'm sure that you will help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's look at 1D1078 then. This will probably refresh your memory of what you said in the Popovic case during your testimony on the 19th of October, 2006. Let's refresh your memory about the date. We need page 64 in e-court, which corresponds to transcript page 2790 in the Popovic case. Line -- lines 17 through 20, and I'll read it out. Your answer -- we need the next page. I apologise. Page 64, which is transcript page 2791. I'll read it out. [In English] "The throwing of the grenades was at the first day, the day of the 8th, in the evening when I had to go south in the enclave. Then the grenades were thrown, and I got back to the headquarters of the Bravo Company, and then I've got to go to Bravo 1." [Interpretation] Does this refresh your memory of it having happened on the 8th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
